findings.evidence: Paragraph 1: Full-time employees who have completed 90 days of continuous service are eligible for the home-office equipment stipend. Paragraph 3: In addition, eligibility for the workspace stipend depends on several details the reviewer checks one at a time.
findings.fix: Use one name for the benefit throughout, or state explicitly the first time the second name appears that it refers to the same stipend already introduced.
findings.violation: The document names the benefit the home-office equipment stipend in one paragraph and the workspace stipend two paragraphs later with no statement that the two names refer to the same benefit, so the reader cannot tell whether a second, separate stipend has just been introduced or the same one has been renamed.

findings.evidence: 71-word sentence, 5 subordinate-clause markers: Similarly, the policy applies to one device per category per employee whenever the benefits team confirms that the role genuinely requires a second device because fieldwork regularly takes the employee away from the single fixed desk that the standard equipment list assumes every applicant has for the whole benefit year while the finance office tracks the second device against the same annual amount that the equipment catalog publishes for each category.
findings.fix: Split the sentence at a subordinate-clause boundary.
findings.violation: The sentence runs to 71 words with 5 subordinate-clause markers, longer than the reader can hold in mind on a single pass.

findings.evidence: The determination of stipend eligibility happens before any payment goes out. The escalation of repeat requests happens automatically within the same quarter.
findings.fix: Name the responsible actor as the subject, for example: the benefits team determines eligibility before releasing payment, and the benefits team escalates repeat requests automatically within the same quarter.
findings.violation: Both sentences making up this section run their action through an abstract noun as the grammatical subject, the determination and the escalation, rather than naming the person or team who determines eligibility or who escalates repeat requests, so a section titled Review Responsibility never actually assigns responsibility to anyone.

findings.evidence: Special Cases, in full: The finance liaison reviews the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year. Staff can request a printed copy from the benefits team at any time. Program Overview and Questions and Updates repeat near-identical sentences under different headings.
findings.fix: Write section-specific content for each heading, and if the budget-tracking note belongs in all three places, state it once and cross-reference it instead of repeating and varying it.
findings.location: Program Overview, Special Cases, and Questions and Updates
findings.violation: Sections headed Program Overview, Special Cases, and Questions and Updates each contain the same recycled pair of sentences about budget or catalog tracking and audit date-stamping instead of content matching their heading; Special Cases in particular describes no special case at all, so a reader finishing that section cannot state what it was actually about or find the guidance the heading promised.

findings.evidence: 71-word sentence: Similarly, the policy applies to one device per category per employee whenever the benefits team confirms that the role genuinely requires a second device because fieldwork regularly takes the employee away from the single fixed desk that the standard equipment list assumes every applicant has for the whole benefit year while the finance office tracks the second device against the same annual amount that the equipment catalog publishes for each category.
findings.fix: Move subordinate clauses and modifiers after the main clause, not between its subject and verb.
findings.violation: At 71 words, with 0 comma-set-off clause(s) and 5 subordinate-clause marker(s), the sentence stacks interruptions between its subject and its main verb instead of holding the main clause together.

findings.evidence: Program Overview: The benefits team tracks the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year. Special Cases: The finance liaison reviews the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year. Questions and Updates: The people operations office tracks the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year.
findings.fix: Name a single consistent owner for this responsibility, or explain how the three roles relate if they are genuinely distinct.
findings.location: Program Overview, Special Cases, and Questions and Updates
findings.violation: Three different named roles, the benefits team, the finance liaison, and the people operations office, are each credited with the identical budget-tracking action in near-identical sentences repeated across three sections, with nothing stating whether these are one body under three names, three bodies duplicating the same duty, or a drafting error.

findings.evidence: Employees must submit the receipt, the manager's approval form, and the original purchase order before the review begins.
findings.fix: Reformat the inline items as a numbered or bulleted list.
findings.violation: The sentence embeds three or more comma- or semicolon-separated parallel items inline rather than presenting them as a formatted list.

findings.evidence: Additionally, employees shall retain receipts for one year after the purchase date.
findings.violation: The sentence states a binding requirement using shall or an indirect requirement phrasing instead of must.

findings.evidence: The finance office conducts an evaluation of every submitted receipt before it approves the amount.
findings.fix: Restate the nominalized noun as the sentence's main verb.
findings.violation: The action is buried inside the noun 'evaluation', carried by a generic support verb, instead of stated as the sentence's own main verb.

findings.evidence: Request Steps (ninth of thirteen sections): Completing the request begins with confirming eligibility, and uploading the receipt. How to Apply (third section): Employees must submit the receipt, the manager's approval form, and the original purchase order before the review begins.
findings.fix: Merge Request Steps into How to Apply, or move it immediately after that section.
findings.location: Request Steps, compared with How to Apply
findings.violation: A short restatement of how to start a request sits in its own section positioned after Approval Timeline, Required Documentation, Reimbursement Amounts, Restrictions and Exceptions, and Terminology Notes, sections that only make sense once a request already exists, instead of appearing next to or inside How to Apply where the reader first needs it.
